title: A Generation Missing Out: One in Four Teenagers Barely Moves
title_zh: 错过运动的一代：四分之一的青少年几乎不运动
source_name: UN News — “15 years of ‘almost no progress’ in getting young people moving: WHO” (4 Nov 2026); WHO news release, 4 Nov 2026
summary_zh: 世界卫生组织 11 月 4 日发布的全球估算显示，全球约四分之一（约 2.4 亿）11–17 岁青少年在过去一周里没有任何一天达到 60 分钟中高强度运动；平均每周只有 2.7 天达标，只有 14% 天天达标。这一水平自 2010 年以来几乎没有变化，女孩比男孩更不爱动。世卫组织认为，解决办法不是让孩子“再努力一点”，而是让学校、街道和社区里的运动变得安全、方便、平常。
paragraphs: One in four teenagers worldwide did not get even one hour of exercise on any day of the previous week, according to new global estimates released by the World Health Organization (WHO) on 4 November. That amounts to roughly 240 million young people aged 11 to 17 who did not complete 60 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity on a single day.

The study, published in The Lancet Global Health, is based on 389 surveys from 140 countries and territories, covering more than 3.2 million adolescents. On average, they reported being active on just 2.7 days a week, and only 14 per cent met the recommended level on all seven days. WHO advises at least an hour a day of anything that raises the heart rate, such as brisk walking or cycling.

Perhaps the most worrying finding is that almost nothing has changed. Activity levels have remained virtually unchanged since 2010, and no country is on track to achieve the global target of a 15 per cent relative reduction in physical inactivity by 2030. "For 15 years, the world has made almost no progress in getting young people moving, and girls are being left furthest behind," said WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus.

The gender gap is strikingly persistent. Twenty-eight per cent of girls reported no active days, compared with 22 per cent of boys, while only 11 per cent of girls were active every day, compared with 17 per cent of boys. There were also stark differences between nations: in some, just 4 per cent of adolescents reported no active days, while in others the figure exceeded 40 per cent.

According to WHO, there is no single explanation for the lack of progress. Physical activity is shaped by where teenagers live, learn, travel and spend their free time. Transport patterns, access to safe public spaces, school environments, cost, social norms and increasingly screen-based lifestyles can all make it harder for them to stay active.

For this reason, WHO argues that the solution is not simply to tell young people to try harder. Instead, it calls for stronger action across education, transport, urban planning, sport and health, such as promoting physical activity in schools and investing in safe walking and cycling routes. Without faster action, the report warns, adolescent inactivity is likely to stay largely unchanged for the rest of the decade.
paragraphs_zh: 根据世界卫生组织（世卫组织）11 月 4 日发布的最新全球估算，全球四分之一的青少年在过去一周里，没有任何一天的运动时间达到哪怕一小时。这意味着约 2.4 亿名 11 至 17 岁的年轻人，连一天都没有完成 60 分钟的中高强度身体活动。
这项研究发表在《柳叶刀·全球健康》上，依据的是来自 140 个国家和地区的 389 项调查，覆盖 320 多万名青少年。平均而言，他们报告自己每周只有 2.7 天是活跃的（达到运动标准），只有 14% 的人一周七天都达到了推荐运动量。世卫组织建议每天至少进行一小时能让心率加快的活动，比如快走或骑自行车。
也许最令人担忧的发现是：情况几乎毫无变化。自 2010 年以来，青少年的运动水平几乎没有改变，而且没有一个国家有望实现“到 2030 年将身体活动不足的比例相对降低 15%”这一全球目标。世卫组织总干事谭德塞说：“15 年来，世界在让年轻人动起来这件事上几乎毫无进展，而女孩被落下得最远。”
性别差距一直显著存在。28% 的女孩报告自己一周中没有一天达标，男孩的这一比例为 22%；每天都达标的女孩只有 11%，男孩则为 17%。各国之间的差异也很悬殊：在一些国家，只有 4% 的青少年报告一周中没有一天达标，而在另一些国家，这一比例超过了 40%。
世卫组织表示，进展缓慢并没有单一的原因。青少年的身体活动受到他们在哪里生活、学习、出行和度过空闲时间的影响。交通方式、能否使用安全的公共空间、学校环境、费用、社会观念，以及越来越以屏幕为中心的生活方式，都可能让他们更难保持运动。
因此，世卫组织认为，解决办法并不只是叫年轻人“再努力一点”。它呼吁在教育、交通、城市规划、体育和卫生等领域采取更有力的行动，例如在学校推广体育活动，投资建设安全的步行和骑行道路。报告警告说，如果不加快行动，在这个十年余下的时间里，青少年运动不足的状况很可能基本不会改变。

questions.prompt: What is the main point of the passage?
options: Teenagers today are far more active than they were in 2010.
Adolescent physical activity remains low worldwide and has hardly improved in 15 years, so WHO wants changes to schools, streets and communities.
Boys are now less active than girls in most countries.
WHO has decided to lower its recommended amount of daily exercise.
questions.explanation: 主旨：全球青少年运动量普遍偏低，15 年来几乎没有改善（女孩更落后），世卫组织因此呼吁改变学校、街道和社区环境，而不只是让孩子自己更努力。

options: It mainly blames teenagers for being lazy.
It believes the problem has already been solved in most countries.
It sees low activity as largely caused by young people's surroundings and daily environment, not just personal choice.
It thinks screen time has no effect on how active teenagers are.
